Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Room 214, Cross Building, Augusta, Maine Thursday, March 13, 2025
Good morning, Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Anne Sedlack, and I am from South Portland, Maine. I am submitting this testimony in support of LD 895, An Act to Support Immersive Outdoor Education by Establishing the Outdoor School for All Maine Students Program.
Many of you might know me as a lobbyist, but I am testifying today as a private citizen. During my freshman year of college, my parents moved to Belfast, and I got a call from my Dad that his colleague's daughter was working at a summer camp in Lincolnville. He told me that I had to apply to the summer camp to make friends in a new state. 18-year-old Anne wanted to stay in Burlington and hang out with her college friends, but the next thing I knew, I was working at a random summer camp in the middle of Lincolnville.
It's cliche, but Tanglewood 4-H Camp changed my life forever. I ended up working there for four years summers, and I met some of my favorite people in the whole world there. I worked in all areas of the camp with children aged five to 18, so I got to witness the magic the outdoors has on children of all ages.
The five-year-old who plays "Meet a Tree," where they put a blindfold on and use all of their other senses to get to know a tree in the forest to try to find it again to the 16-year-old who has never been on the water before and ends the canoe trip by waking up at 3:00 am to travel down the final part of the St. George river to catch the tide out to the ocean. These children learn that the outdoors is our greatest asset. They know how nature can calm their brain down and be a place to find peace amongst a favorite birch tree or the babbling river.
But the reality is that the kids who attended this summer camp had parents who could afford to send them or had parents/teachers who knew how to take advantage of the various scholarships available for Maine students. Scholarships are beneficial but also a barrier to ensuring that all children can access the outdoors since there are limited slots and often a lengthy application to be considered.
This bill, and the previous iteration of it, LD 1817, from the 131st Legislature, which had over 110 cosponsors, passed unanimously out of this Committee, through the House and Senate, and got stuck on the funding table, ensure that ALL Maine children have equitable access to the outdoors for a two night and three-day trip during their school year. I can assure you that this experience will, like me, also change so many children's lives forever. It is a privilege to access the outdoors in such an immersive way, and we owe it to our children to ensure they can all access the outdoors.
I would be happy to answer any questions.
Best, Anne Sedlack

Testimony of
DANA A. DORAN Executive Director Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast
Before the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry on LD 550, An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential
Learning in Public Schools
Thursday, March 20, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, my name is Dana Doran, and I am the Executive Director of the Professional Logging Contractors of the Northeast (PLC). The PLC is a regional non-profit educational organization that promotes professional logging and trucking throughout the Northeast, predominately in the state of Maine.
As background, the PLC was created in 1995 to give logging and associated trucking contractors a voice in a rapidly changing forest products industry. As of 2021, logging and trucking contractors in Maine employed over 3,000 people directly and were indirectly responsible for the creation of an additional 2,500 jobs. This employment and the investments that contractors make contributed $582 million to the state's economy. Our membership, which includes over 200 contractor members in the state of Maine and an additional 125 associate members, is responsible for more than 80% of Maine's annual timber harvest.
Thank you for providing me the opportunity to testify on behalf of our membership in support of LD 550, An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools. The PLC would like to thank the sponsor for bringing this legislation forward.
By establishing the Maine Experiential Education Program within the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry, and managing a grant program, schools will have an opportunity to deliver educational experiences they might not otherwise been able to provide. Although significant strides have been made in recent years, there is still more the state can do to provide learning experiences for students who don't fit the mold of the traditional public school system.
Today, every child does not learn the same nor do they all fit the mold of a traditional classroom learning environment. Programs like that which is proposed in this bill, can stimulate the creative mind of students to find their passion.

Currently, there are only five CTE schools in the state that include forestry education. However, over the last 10 years, the PLC has participated in the Maine Forest Collaborative, a nontraditional education program that works to educate students on Maine's natural resources. Part of the collaborative's mission states, "All Maine Forest Collaborative students are experiencing real-world, relevant learning opportunities, bringing them closer to understanding the careers available in our rural forest-based communities, and developing the skills necessary for success in those careers." It is vital to have programs like this to ensure one of our heritage industries is protected and well positioned for future generations.
Although it doesn't apply directly to this potential program, in 2015, we helped create the Mechanized Logging Operations and Forest Trucking (MLOFT) program, in partnership with the Maine Community College System. Currently, MLOFT is accepting applications for its 9th year. MLOFT gives students an opportunity to work on a real logging site using state of the art mechanized logging equipment. In addition to being trained on all the equipment, the students will also leave the program with a Class A, CDL license. Once the class is complete, we work with local contractors to help guide program graduates to employment opportunities available within the industry. MLOFT is an example of the benefits of non-traditional education that could be created if this legislation is passed out of this Committee.
The PLC appreciates the sponsor for continuing to explore avenues to enhance opportunities of alternative learning here in Maine. The forest is one of Maine's greatest natural resources and by educating more young people about forestry, it is a vital way to continue responsible and sustainable management in the future.
Thank you for your consideration and I urge you to vote ought to pass on this bill.
10037182:
Testimony Presented by The Ecology School in Support of LD 550
Thursday, March 13, 2025 @ 1pm - An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools
Good afternoon Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Agriculture, Conservation & Forestry Committee:
My name is Drew Dumsch, and I am a resident of Saco, Maine and President & CEO of The Ecology School, a nonprofit outdoor school and environmental living & learning center located at the historic 313-acre River Bend Farm on the Saco River in rural southwest Saco. I am also a member of the Maine Outdoor School for All Network which is a state-wide collaboration of experiential learning centers offering multi-day overnight programs for students and classroom teachers throughout Maine. For 26 years The Ecology School has had the honor to work with thousands of Maine students and their classroom teachers to support their experiential learning in the curriculum areas of agriculture, conservation, forestry, environmental science and sustainability.
LD 550-- An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools-- will support innovative experiential education for more Maine students and ensure that Maine K-12 schools increase opportunities to partner with Maine nonprofit education providers of farm, forestry and conservation education programs. Given this history and legacy of our state's natural resources and the amazing opportunities that learning outside provides to Maine students, I'm excited that this bill will support more children learning where their food comes from and even learning to grow their own food. Understanding the importance of agriculture, forestry and conservation to Maine's economy and workforce is an important outcome of supporting more agriculture-based, experiential education for Maine students, classroom teachers and schools.
LD 550 will also support the Maine Farm & Sea to School Network, an amazing experiential education initiative that brings together partners such as UMaine Cooperative Extension, Maine Agriculture in the Classroom, Maine School Garden Network, USDA, and the Maine Department of Education to convene a summer institute that benefits entire school districts with experiential education training for teachers, students, school administrators and school food service staff. The Ecology School has been honored to host the first three Maine Farm and Sea to School Institutes at our River Bend Farm campus and we look forward to hosting the next Institute this summer.
I also appreciate the experiential learning piece of this bill because I've been working on the LD 895 Outdoor School legislation that you held a hearing on this morning. As someone who has been active for years with the Maine Environmental Education Association, I can attest to the many strong partnerships between public schools and nonprofit experiential education providers that exist throughout the state. Unfortunately, given current school budgets, funding for experiential agriculturebased learning is limited even though studies have shown that the health, learning and behavior of children all improve through outdoor focused, hands-on learning in gardens and farms.
I strongly urge this Committee to consider and pass all legislation that supports getting our children more experiential learning in agriculture, conservation and forestry.
Thank you,
Drew Dumsch -- Co-Founder, President & CEO -- The Ecology School River Bend Farm -- 184 Simpson Road -- Saco, Maine 04072
ph: 207.294.2299 -- Drew@TheEcologySchool.org -- www.TheEcologySchool.org
10037227:
Testimony of Garrett Mason In Support of LD 550
An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools
Senator Talbot-Ross, Representative Pluecker, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture Conservation and Forestry. My name is Garrett Mason, I am a resident of Lisbon Falls, and am a Partner at Dirigo Public Affairs. I am here today representing our client, the Maine Farm Bureau and am here in support of LD 550.
At its heart, LD 550 invests in children by giving them hands-on learning experiences in growing food, understanding where it comes from, and appreciating the work that goes into producing it. In a time when many young people are disconnected from the land and the food they eat, this legislation will help schools create programs that reconnect them with Maine's agricultural roots. By supporting school gardens, farm-to-school programs, and outdoor experiential education, we can give students the knowledge and confidence to grow their own food, make informed choices about nutrition, and develop a deeper appreciation for the land that sustains us.
These lessons in agriculture are about more than just growing food; they are about self-sufficiency and lifelong skills. A child who learns how to plant a seed, care for a garden, and harvest fresh food will carry those skills into adulthood. They will understand the value of hard work, the importance of sustainability, and the rewards of providing for themselves and their communities. In an era where food security is a growing concern, equipping the next generation with the ability to grow their own food is not just an educational benefit--it is a life skill that fosters independence.
Maine has a proud farming heritage, but as fewer young people enter agriculture, we must do more to ensure the next generation understands the role of farming and food production in our daily lives. LD 550 will not only introduce children to these essential concepts but will also create pathways for them to explore careers in agriculture, food science, and environmental stewardship. By giving students hands-on experiences in farming, fishing, and gardening, we are opening doors for them to consider futures in these vital industries.
Beyond the skills gained, LD 550 strengthens the bond between Maine's farms and its communities. By increasing local food procurement in schools, this bill also creates new opportunities for Maine's farmers and fishermen to provide fresh, local products to students. It fosters a cycle where students not only learn about agriculture but actively participate in

supporting it--building an understanding of the hard work that goes into feeding our communities.
This bill is an investment in our children, our local food systems, and our agricultural future. By supporting LD 550, we are ensuring that Maine's students gain the knowledge, confidence, and skills to be more self-reliant and better stewards of the land. The Maine Farm Bureau urges the Committee to vote Ought to Pass and help bring this vital program to our schools.
Thank you for your time and consideration. I welcome any questions and appreciate your support of Maine's students and agricultural heritage.
10041405:
MOFGA Comments In Support Of
LD 550 - An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools
and
LD 895 - An Act to Support Immersive Outdoor Education by Establishing the Outdoor School for All Maine Students Program
March 13, 2025
Dear Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker and members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry,
On behalf of the Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association (MOFGA), I am submitting comments in support of both LD 550 - An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools and LD 895 - An Act to Support Immersive Outdoor Education by Establishing the Outdoor School for All Maine Students Program.
A broad-based community, MOFGA is transforming our food system by supporting farmers, empowering people to feed their communities, and advocating for an organic future. We extend quality, agriculture-based education to young people across Maine. We're working hard to create opportunities for Maine's next generation of farmers. MOFGA certifies 537 organic farms and processing operations representing more than $120 million in sales. Each of these farmers is a Maine businessperson for whom economic health and environmental health are interdependent. While MOFGA envisions a future of healthy ecosystems, communities, people, and economies sustained by the practices of organic agriculture, we attribute our success to collaboration and outreach to growers across the management spectrum.
We are excited about the prospects of both of these bills. LD 550 seeks to create the Maine Experiential Education Program within the Department of Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry provide Maine schools with outdoor and experiential hands-on learning opportunities related to gardens, food and agriculture. The program would improve students' health and academic, physical and emotional development, and would provide related professional development opportunities for educators. LD 895 would, under the leadership of Maine's Cooperative Extension Service, create the Outdoor School for All Maine Students Program and Fund, providing immersive outdoor education for Maine's 4th through 8th graders. We are particularly excited about the opportunities that these initiatives would provide for encouraging students to learn about healthy, local, organic and sustainable food and agriculture systems and we would be happy to engage in this program where possible.
At MOFGA we offer garden-based education to members of the public year-round, both in-person and online, as well as at the Common Ground Fair every September. We partner with the Maine School Garden Network, where one our Community Education Director sits on the board. Since 1998, we have been welcoming school groups to our Common Ground Education Center where they participate in projects in our gardens and orchards, including many groups of students. Students from the Ecology Learning Center, Ironwood and Maine Academy of Natural Sciences are regular visitors and participants in our educational programs.

207-568-4142 � www.mofga.org

PO Box 170, Unity, ME 04988

We are well aware of how meaningful these programs are in terms of enabling more effective learning and better behavioral outcomes for students. Once a school has the chance to trial a garden program and begins to see some of these outcomes manifest themselves - for instance, lower instances of behavioral referrals or more effective science learning - it will likely become easier for them to justify the continued costs of such programs even after grant funds have expired after three years.
We also see many connections between the program that this bill would initiate and our goal of supporting the growth of a healthier food system for all.
A core part of building a healthy food system is building awareness about our current agricultural system. Where does our food come from? What does it look and feel like to be a farmer in Maine today? What does it actually cost to produce quality food - that is, food grown in a way that allows farmers and farmworkers to make a decent living, and that respects ecosystem health and conserves natural resources? These are questions that we need more Mainers to reflect on regularly. LD 550 and LD 895 could support the growth of a healthy and fair food system, as it could help kids build connections between the food that they, and their communities, produce and the food that they prepare and eat.
Exposure to gardening in young kids and teenagers can have lifelong effects perhaps prompting an interest in farm work, forestry or landscaping as a meaningful career, or an interest (paired with the ability) to grow food for one's own family, boosting their health and food security. Both have tremendous value.
We also see this as a justice and equity issue. We know that better-funded school districts are more likely to be able to fund their own gardener educator positions without any grant assistance, offering their students the opportunity to reap all the health, learning and behavioral benefits of this programming. But children in all parts of Maine deserve a quality education. This grant program would help level the playing field so that kids in communities of all kinds could benefit from these opportunities.
Thank you for your consideration and support of this important legislation.
Respectfully submitted,
Heather Spalding Deputy Director - Maine Organic Farmers and Gardeners Association

10036848:
Lisa DePasqual Brooklin LD 550
Testimony of Lisa DePasqual of Brooklin before the 132st Legislature's Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry
Dear members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry. My name is Lisa DePasqual, I am a resident of Brooklin, and I am here today to express my support of LD 550 - An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools
I believe so strongly in the importance of agricultural literacy that I volunteer hundreds of hours each year to running a community garden in Brooklin. In addition to private allotments where town residents can grow their own crops, we have an area we call "teaching plots" where we teach eachother about growing food and share the produce with the community.
When the garden gets to host students from the Brooklin School, it is rewarding for all of us. Kindergartners digging for worms and pulling carrots engages them with soil health and counting the harvest. First graders planting peas in the spring so they can be shared at our town's 4th of July picnic is a lesson in following instructions, developing fine motor skills, and contributing to town life. One year, when the garden needed an arched trellis for growing cucumbers, we turned it into a math and engineering exercise for older students. But, sadly, the 3-8 grade classes typically do not make time for even the occasional garden session. Their days are packed full with "meeting the standards". This has been a sadness to me, as I believe that developing an appreciation for food production and hard work IS an essential component of a good education.
LD 550 promises, if I understand it correctly, to give curriculum support and funding for agricultural and experiential learning. It means that teachers will have the backing they need to prioritize agricultural literacy. I applaud this bill, and I ask you to support LD 550.
10036975:
Molly DellaRoman Brooklin LD 550
Molly DellaRoman Brooklin, Maine March 11, 2025
Dear Members of the Committee on Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry,
Thank you for the opportunity to submit written testimony on the behalf of LD 550. My name is Molly DellaRoman and I am writing today to express full support for LD 550 on the behalf of the Brooklin School, the Brooklin Food Corps and Brooklin's Climate Response Committee.
As chair of the Brooklin Food Corps, I wish to share with you the story of a long-term partnership between the Brooklin School and several organizations in Brooklin. In 1999, the Brooklin Youth Corps (BYC) was founded, and as part of this summer job-oriented program, land from a family adjacent to the school was donated for a school garden. Over time, an orchard and greenhouse was installed on the school's property. Until 2019, the garden was maintained and funded by the staff and volunteers of the BYC Steering Committee. Students and teachers worked in the garden during the school year, while providing food for the school's cafeteria. In the summer months, the garden was worked by the children enrolled in the BYC, learning how to grow food and also how to market and sell it at the local farmers' market. Over the years, several of those students went on to volunteer and work on local farms.
Responding to new challenges with the Covid-19 pandemic in 2021, the BYC evolved to become the Brooklin Food Corps (BFC). This all volunteer-run organization still maintains the garden, which has expanded to become a community garden, with dedicated days for the students to come and learn what it takes to plan a garden, get their hands dirty, taste the food they grow and help harvest for local food relief programs. The orchard is still being maintained and expanded by the BFC. Cider pressing is a favorite of the students every fall. This spring, in collaboration with the school's newly formed Eco-Club (an after-school nature immersion program), Brooklin's Climate Response Committee, and the BFC, a new program will be launched - Growing Up With Trees. Each first grader will be gifted a tree that they will help raise in a tree nursery being installed at the school. As 7th graders, they will harvest and plant the tree in a public or private space of their choosing. One can only imagine what such an invaluable experience may inspire in our students.
This town loves supporting our school in any way we can. We know our teachers are called to perform tremendous feats every day and they excel at it. They also would love the chance to help students to experience even more of the natural beauty and resources that our unique rural, coastal town has to offer. The chance to have a paid position to help organize and communicate with all parties would help these programs to run as efficiently as possible for the school and give our students the best chance they have to protect and preserve Maine's future.
Thank you for the opportunity to share my perspective with the Committee, Molly DellaRoman

AN ACT TO SUPPORT OUTDOOR, AGRICULTURAL-BASED AND HANDS-ON EXPERIENTIAL LEARNING IN PUBLIC SCHOOLS
March 13, 2025
Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and members of the Agriculture, Conservation and Forestry Committee, I am Robbie Feinberg, the director of communications and government relations for the Maine School Management Association, testifying on behalf of the legislative committee of the Maine School Boards Association in support of L.D. 550, An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools. We represent more than 1,700 school board members across all regions of Maine.
Our members believe this bill takes a constructive, supportive approach that could provide our schools and students with additional capacity and resources to develop new approaches to boost student engagement and proficiency.
Across the state, many schools are already working to develop the outdoor, agricultural -based and hands-on experiential learning experiences described in this bill. As just a few examples: � MSAD 17 holds engineering and science classes at nearby Roberts Farm. � MSAD 1 in Presque Isle operates an educational farm supplying produce sent to
local stores and restaurants. � Maine Teacher of the Year Becky Hallowell puts outdoor learning at the center of
her educational approach in her "Outdoor Wonderful Learning Space" along the Sheepscot River.
Studies show that nature and outdoor-based learning are beneficial for our students. It improves student engagement, decreases negative behaviors, and serves as a powerful alternative to technology and social media.
While many Maine schools have embraced this approach, we know many districts do not have the funding to create or expand their own efforts. L.D. 550 would provide crucial resources to schools to jumpstart these efforts. And by operating as a grant program - rather than a state mandate - it will allow districts to choose to opt in if they want to.
This would preserve local curriculum control and provide useful financial incentives to help districts looking to move in this direction. It would also seek funding from private, nonprofit, or federal sources, putting less pressure on state and local taxpayers. Our association is fully in support of this approach to funding, and we believe it will provide valuable resources that will boost student engagement and academic success. We urge you to support L.D. 550.

March 13, 2023 Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry
FoodCorps Testimony in Support of LD 550 An Act to Support Outdoor,
Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools
Senator Ross, Representative Pluecker, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry,
My name is Ryan Parker, and I am the Maine Impact and Partnerships Lead for
FoodCorps which is a national nonprofit organization which partners with schools all around the country to provide students with experiential learning opportunities
tied to food, cooking, and gardening. For the past 14 years, we have worked with
Maine communities from Portland to the Katahdin Region, Indian Township to Eustis, to provide hands-on lessons that help students learn better, and get excited about eating fruits and vegetables and support school nutrition staff in getting
nourishing meals on school trays. l am a lifelong Mainer and l live in Newport with my family Where, until recently, l sen/ed on the RSU 19 School Board, and now coach young athletes at all levels. I am here today on behalf of FoodCorps to ask
you to support passage of LD 550, An Act to Support Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools.
Thank you to Senator Guerin and her cosponsors for introducing this important opportunity for the schools and children throughout Maine, and for supporting
experiential learning.
Many people intuitively understand that humans of all ages learn best by doing. We do
not learn to ride a bike by reading books about it, or hunt by doing worksheets, or drive by watching videos. All of those things are certainly useful learning tools, but most people, and certainly the vast majority of children, must use their bodies along with their
minds to actually learn. Many educators and advocates have long been calling for less stationary time at a desk and more outdoor, tactile, and movement based learning
opportunities. Most people, including most teachers, intuitively understand the reality that experiential learning is most beneficial to students. But, there has long been a reluctance
to engage in teaching experientially due to many barriers, most of which come down to capacity. Because of what our public education system was originally designed to do, and because of the way it has subsequently developed over the past century, teachers

FOODCORPS
are not taught in our colleges to engage in experiential learning. Those teachers that do
teach this way will be the first to tell you managing an outdoor classroom and even hands-on activities inside is much different than managing indoor, sit-down, traditional
classrooms. lt is harder, which is saying something because teaching is already very challenging, takes more prep-time, and often involves clean-up after lessons. lt involves
considerations around how children are dressed, what type of footwear they have on a
given day, and having materials that can withstand weather and physical movement. For
years many organizations and individuals have worked to chip away at these hesitations
with resources, professional development, and full programs designed to help those
early adopters who both recognize the value of experiential education, and want to take advantage of it. lt was long, hard, slow work to expand the educational paradigm.
But the covid pandemic, for all its disruption and tragedy, carried with it the silver lining
that many Maine schools were forced to quickly create new systems to educate our
children in outdoor spaces where airflow is far superior to that in even our most modern
school buildings. Federal Covid relief funding made much of this possible because it included hundreds of thousands of dollars schools had to use exclusively to create
outdoor learning spaces. Most schools chose to invest in school gardens, school
orchards, hoop and greenhouses, and pavilions. This makes sense given that over 80%
of experiential learning that happens in l\/laine is tied to school gardening. importantly,
many schools hired specific people to help students and teachers take advantage of this new infrastructure; helping teachers connect the outdoor growing and learning spaces to existing standards and curriculum for all subjects from Fine Arts, to Language Arts, from
Math and Science to Social Studies.
While a select and small handful of schools have long been engaged in this type of education, the pandemic introduced it to many more. LD 550 fills a critical need to help schools begin to take advantage of the realities most have seen with experiential learning during the pandemic. This need has always been there but is
now urgent. Covid relief money has disappeared from all school districts across the country. This has become known as the "Covid cliff." School districts throughout Maine working through this, some better than others. Experiential and outdoor learning programs that began during the pandemic are among the most
universally valued. But schools need help to continue outdoor experiential learning programs.
The reasons for this are simple. Over recent decades, science has finally begun to prove what many have long known, and what dozens of schools around Maine have just begun

FOODCORPS
to experience. Specifically, children do better, by every measure, when they can learn by doing, particularly if it is a natural setting (outside). Children make deeper learning connections when they can learn experientially. Children's behavior improves when they can get outside, meaning fewer office referrals and disciplinary actions, which means our principals can spend more of their time developing curricula and evaluating teachers. Mental health improves when children (and adults) are outside. These and other facts are well documented in dozens of studies, only a partiality of which are highlighted in the
list accompanying this testimony.
In addition to the timeliness of this legislation, LD 550 is well-crafted because it does not force anything on schools. l\/laine is a local control state and, as a school board member
myself, I have strong opinions about local control. This bill provides support for
experiential learning, but only to those districts who choose to use it. In other words, this
is not an educational mandate. Under this language, districts are free to choose to partner with the Department, or not. And if they do, they are free to stick to their own curriculum, connecting it to outdoor and experiential learning as they see best fits their communities. There is nothing in this legislation that dictates what must be taught. And, garden and other experiential education provides nearly infinite flexibility to meet schools where they want to go.
Perhaps the most interesting, and useful part of this legislation is the fact that it strikes
an often difficult to achieve level of support. Some programs provide one time support which may allow for an exciting project to be created, but not sustained. Indeed, Covid
relief funds were a good example. They were required by law to be spent on outdoor infrastructure like greenhouses. But there was no money to deal with the maintenance, use, and connecting this infrastructure to curricula. Other types of support become a crutch to achieve that sustainability. This legislation is based on the old proverb that it is better to teach someone to fish than give them fish. LD 550 provides for a gradual build up of programming which will then be sustained by the district itself. lt will also, therefore, provide an opportunity for all schools that are interested in this type of program to take advantage of it relatively quickly as the state support can shift from one community to another in succession around Maine.
l
FoodCorps' has long focused on this type of work. Our goal in Maine is always to help schools build outdoor learning spaces, learn to use them, and expand their use by
teachers and students so they can realize all the benefits outlined above. We build these

FOODCORPS
partnerships with the exit strategy in mind at the outset. We help districts to become
self-sufficient, meaning they will continue to expand and use their experiential learning
programs long after FoodCorps moves on to help other communities. As such, we work
to build support in districts for the creation of positions like those outlined in this
legislation. When FoodCorps partners with a school district, we usually plan to be there for two to six years, depending on many factors including size of district, level of existing infrastructure, culture of use, and more. With our limited resources, We are only currently
in 7 communities throughout Maine. Since FoodCorps' inception just over a decade ago,
we have served in several communities. There are approximately 192 school districts in
the state. At the current rate, it would take FoodCorps nearly 800 years to reach every
school, and every kid most of whom would thrive if they could grow up with experiential
education as the norm.
l\/laine is a leader in the realm of Farm to School programming, which means schools
would have a lot of support if they were to participate in this program. Indeed, no other
state brings a focus on the Sea to their programming. FoodCorps is a proud member of the robust and long-lived Farm and Sea to School Network, composed of organizations and individuals who support experiential learning based on gardens, food, fisheries, and
agriculture, two of Maine's most important industries. FoodCorps joins our partners in this network and beyond in recognizing the incredible value of experience to the development of young minds which grow into thoughtful, contributing citizens. l urge you
to vote ought to pass on LD 550. l am happy to answer any questions you may have, and l will do my best to provide any additional information you may require. l am happy
to be of service when you discuss this bill in the work session.

Thank you,

March 13, 2025

Senator Talbot Ross, Representative Pluecker, and Members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Agriculture, Conservation, and Forestry:
My name is Senator Stacey Guerin and I am here today presenting LD 550, "An Act to Support
Outdoor, Agricultural-based and Hands-on Experiential Learning in Public Schools." This is an amended version of a bill that was considered and unanimously supported by this Committee in the 131st Legislature. Like the original, the purpose of this bill is to help local school districts and individual schools throughout Maine create positions that will allow for the expansion of experiential, hands-on education right in the schools and communities where kids are for at least 175 days every year.

As a former teacher myself, I can attest to the fact that kids learn better, have fewer behavior issues, and pay attention more easily when they can be active and, whenever possible, get outside
to learn. I personally maintained a school nature walk at the elementary school where I taught.
The children loved it and followed the seasonal changes with enthusiasm. But, I also know how
hard teachers work and that the additional requirements to make outdoor and experiential learning happen are sometimes beyond their capacity or even interest. Many times I traded
classes with other teachers to give their students an opportunity to be guided by me on the nature
trail. This bill's provisions include not only the additional effort and focus needed to connect experiential learning spaces and infrastructure to the curriculum, but also the maintenance of that
infrastructure. This is where LD 550 comes in.

I firmly believe local communities support the concept of experiential learning, as is evidenced by the fact that some districts across Maine have been able to create positions, whether they be certified teachers, ed techs, or coach positions, to create connections between outdoor and handson learning spaces and the curriculum our teachers deliver in math, science, social studies, English, art, music, and even phys ed. But right now, this is limited to a handful of districts that are either more financially well-off or are fortunate to exist in a place where there is non-profit
support.

However, all children learn better by doing, and given the possibilities that exist in all parts of Maine relative to our natural resources and beautiful settings, these limitations should not hold back students anywhere in our great state.
